extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty and administrators responsible for assessing and improving undergraduate mathematics programs
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and carrying out an assessment cycle for an undergraduate mathematics major: set learning goals, align curriculum and instructional strategies, select and implement assessment methods, collect and evaluate data, and use results to improve the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning goal clarity and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning goals should state what students who complete the major should be able to do (for example: read and understand mathematical statements, make and test conjectures, construct and write proofs using direct/indirect methods, counterexamples, induction; read standard mathematical literature and judge validity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete, actionable goal language that can be linked to courses and assessment methods. Example goal given with emphasis on proof skills and reading mathematical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of courses, assignments, and activities to goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which parts of courses are specifically aimed at helping students reach each goal, which student assignments help reach the goal, what students should do outside courses, what faculty should do to help students, what additional facilities are needed, and what learning research suggests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed questions as a template when making goals specific to a degree program; reference particular courses and activities when mapping strategies to goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional strategy across curriculum years
rubrics_metrics.description: Define strategies across years (e.g., first-year: encounter theorems with instructor justifications and finding counterexamples; second/third years: learn fundamental logic and construct proofs as homework/exams; third/fourth years: formulate conjectures, find proofs/disproofs, present and critique orally and in writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how skills are introduced, practiced, critiqued, and advanced year-by-year; include written and oral presentation practice and critique by mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine broad, manageable assessment areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Select areas of student accomplishment and departmental effectiveness to document (examples: curriculum (core and major), instructional process, co-curricular activities, retention within major/institution, success after graduation; possibly advising and campus environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Areas should be as broad as can be managed and should be chosen based on learning goals and strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign responsibility for assessment areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility for each chosen area of assessment should be clearly assigned (e.g., mathematics faculty assess learning in the mathematics major; the college may assess the core curriculum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document who is responsible for data collection, analysis, and follow-up for each area to ensure accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match assessment methods to type of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose assessment methods that reflect the type of learning to be measured (e.g., GRE for preparation for graduate school; attitude survey for aptitude for lifelong learning; objective paper-and-pencil exam for specific content knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the construct you want to measure and select tools appropriate to that construct rather than defaulting to convenient measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a combination of assessment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments will typically use a combination of methods, selected in view of local program needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine multiple methods to capture multidimensional learning; the document lists eight types of methods as common options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests can be objective or subjective, multiple-choice or free-response, written or oral, nationally standardized (e.g., GRE, ETS Major Field Achievement Test) or locally generated; most effective in measuring specific knowledge and its basic meaning and use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select test types according to what is being measured; recognize limitations for complex or process-oriented learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys (written or interview-based) can sample students, faculty, employers, and alumni; can be administered in courses, at graduation, or when students change majors to gather reasons and perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys to capture attitudes, expectations, and perceptions; tailor the target group and timing to the question being asked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation reports (checklists and ratings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation reports use checklists of skills and abilities completed by faculty, peers, or employers; self-evaluations may be used but are generally less valuable; grades are fundamental evaluation reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop standardized checklists/protocols; prefer objective external evaluations when possible; document rubric and rater training to increase objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios are collections of student work compiled under faculty supervision following a departmental protocol; contents may include homework, exams, writing samples, independent project reports, and background info and should reflect student progress through the major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sort contents by category or year, review curriculum objectives to decide what to include, allow student choice for some samples, and ensure consistent protocols for collection and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays can reveal writing skills in mathematics as well as subject knowledge (e.g., assigned summaries of read articles); essays should contribute to learning and can be included in portfolios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design essay tasks that are pedagogically meaningful (e.g., model summaries by faculty followed by student summaries) and assess both content and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary / capstone courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary courses (capstones, senior seminars, or research seminars) are designed to cover and connect ideas across the major and provide good summary information about learning in the major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use performance in these courses as an integrative assessment of program-level learning outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral presentations demonstrate speaking ability, confidence, and subject knowledge; presentations on mathematical articles or projects can be assessed and peer discussion can serve both learning and assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include oral components where appropriate and use peer discussion as formative assessment; assess both content mastery and communication skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue with students
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect student attitudes, expectations, and opinions through evaluations, interviews, advising interactions, seminars, student journals, and informal interactions; in-depth interviews of project participants can provide insight into learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple dialogue formats to gather qualitative evidence and triangulate with other measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure student cooperation and provide varied opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Student cooperation and involvement are essential; assessment methods should provide varied ways for students to show knowledge and skills and should allow alternative presentation and response modes to accommodate diverse needs while supporting uniform standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate goals, methods, and portfolio contents to students; ideally students should be able to articulate progress toward goals and produce an exit essay reflecting their learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address motivation when assessments don't affect progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Some assessment measures may not affect individual students' progress and therefore motivation to participate may be low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider non-evaluative rewards or incentives to encourage participation in assessments that are primarily programmatic rather than grading-related.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful record keeping and data management
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep careful, well-planned records anticipating future assessment needs; additional storage space or a dedicated computer database may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan data retention and formats; store longitudinal records for tracking majors through the program and after graduation; ensure data are evaluable relative to goals and objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and revise standards and criteria for evaluating data
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and criteria for evaluating data should be set and modified as better information becomes available, including longitudinal data gathered through tracking majors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop explicit evaluation rubrics/benchmarks and update them as institutional data and comparisons inform practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative evaluation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate data via comparisons with goals and preset benchmarks, over time, to national or regional norms, to faculty/student/employer expectations, to data at similar institutions, and to other majors within the institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external data sources (e.g., CIRP freshman survey, ACT College Outcomes Measures) where appropriate and perform longitudinal comparisons for program evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign a core group for consistency in interpreting data
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign a core group of departmental faculty members to facilitate consistency in interpreting assessment data, especially over periods of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the core group to maintain consistent standards, norms, and interpretive practices across assessment cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track students longitudinally
rubrics_metrics.description: Track students from application through post-graduation, recording interests at application, high school records, curricular/extracurricular records, advanced degrees, employment, and attitudes to document long-term program effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longitudinal tracking enables valid long-term comparisons and effectiveness studies; collect consistent identifiers and key datapoints to support follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the effectiveness of strategies, methods, and processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Before beginning the next assessment cycle, ask whether current strategies are effective, what should be added or subtracted, what curriculum/instruction changes are needed, whether methods measure important learning for all students, and whether more/different methods are needed; review the assessment process itself for realism, focus, documentation, and record-keeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these reflective questions to close the assessment loop and to plan changes for the next cycle; document decisions and rationale for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use assessment results to improve the program continuously
rubrics_metrics.description: Use documented evidence of student learning and how it was achieved to guide improvements for future students; improvements should be implemented whenever needs are identified, not only at periodic intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on valid inferences from evidence to identify actionable improvements; maintain faculty engagement in interpreting results and implementing changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make valid inferences about student performance and learning processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine valid inferences about student performances based on evidence gathered; evidence should show not only what students have learned but what processes contributed to the learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessment and data collection to illuminate causal or contributory instructional processes; use multidimensional evidence to support claims about learning.
